title: Chest pain, friction rub, and ECG changes
presentation: A 54-year-old man presents to the ED with sudden onset sharp chest pain radiating to his left shoulder, worse with deep inspiration and lying flat, better sitting forward. He denies cough, fever, dyspnea, nausea, or vomiting. His vital signs are BP 130/75, HR 110, RR 22, Temp 37.1C, SpO2 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals clear lungs, no JVD or edema, but a grade 2/6 pericardial friction rub heard best at the left lower sternal border. EKG shows diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression.

stages.label: History
stages.text: He reports the pain started acutely 2 hours ago. He has no significant past medical history except for hypertension treated with lisinopril. He takes no other medications. He works as a software engineer and denies recent travel, sick contacts, or known exposures. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He denies recent trauma or surgery.
stages.prompt: What is your initial diagnostic approach and what key questions should you ask?
stages.learner_goal: Recognize features suggestive of acute pericarditis and differentiate it from ACS.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: Vital signs show tachycardia and tachypnea. Lung exam is unremarkable. Cardiac exam reveals a loud, triphasic pericardial friction rub. Neurological exam is normal. There are no signs of heart failure.
stages.prompt: Does the physical exam change your differential? Commit to your top 2 diagnoses based on the history and exam.
stages.learner_goal: Identify classic signs of acute pericarditis and consider alternative causes of chest pain.

stages.label: Results
stages.text: EKG confirms diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression. Troponin level is negative. Chest X-ray shows a normal cardiac silhouette without cardiomegaly or pulmonary edema. CBC shows WBC count of 8.5 k/uL with normal differential. BMP shows potassium of 4.2 mEq/L and BUN/Creatinine ratio of 12.5.
stages.prompt: With the history, exam, and initial results, what is the most likely diagnosis? What test definitively confirms it?
stages.learner_goal: Synthesize the clinical picture to arrive at the diagnosis of acute pericarditis.

key_clues: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward
Diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression on EKG

distractors.name: Myocardial Infarction (MI)
distractors.why_not: Negative troponin, characteristic EKG changes (diffuse vs localized), pleuritic nature of pain

distractors.name: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
distractors.why_not: Absence of dyspnea, pleuritic pain less common, EKG changes atypical for PE, friction rub absent

distractors.name: Pneumonia
distractors.why_not: Absence of fever, cough, consolidation on CXR, EKG changes atypical

distractors.name: Costochondritis
distractors.why_not: Pain typically reproducible on palpation, lacks systemic signs, EKG changes absent

distractors.name: Aortic Dissection
distractors.why_not: Pain often tearing/ripping, absence of pulse deficit or neurological findings, EKG changes atypical

rubric.description: Characterizes the chest pain as sharp and pleuritic
rubric.concept: Classic description of pericarditic chest pain

rubric.description: Notes the presence of a pericardial friction rub

rubric.concept: Specific EKG findings highly suggestive of pericarditis
Rules out some causes like MI with heart failure or pneumonia

rubric.description: Considers MI and PE as important differentials
rubric.concept: Initial differential diagnosis always includes life-threatening conditions like MI and PE

rubric.description: Identifies EUS as the definitive test
rubric.concept: Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis, assesses for effusion size, and rules out tamponade
First-line treatment for uncomplicated acute pericarditis
Essential due to potential for hemodynamic compromise

management_summary: Start NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 600mg TID) or aspirin (81mg daily). Add colchicine (0.5mg BID) for 3 days to prevent recurrence. Monitor for signs of hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, elevated JVP). If symptoms worsen or fever develops, suspect early tamponade or purulent pericarditis and obtain urgent echocardiogram. Avoid fluoroquinolones and renin inhibitors (like ACEi/ARBs) due to increased risk of TIAs.
teaching_points: Acute pericarditis classically presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward and improved by sitting forward.
A pericardial friction rub is pathognomonic but may be transient.
The EKG shows diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression, mimicking STEMI but with different morphology and reciprocal changes.
Troponin levels are typically normal unless there is associated myocarditis.
A normal chest X-ray helps rule out pneumonia or large pleural effusions.
Key differentials include MI, PE, and costochondritis. Always consider life-threatening conditions first.
Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis, assesses for effusion size, and rules out tamponade.
Treatment involves NSAIDs or aspirin, plus colchicine to reduce recurrence rates.
Monitor patients closely for signs of developing pericardial effusion or tamponade.
references: FesmEndocarditis Society Guidelines for the Prevention of Perioperative Complications Related to Valvular Heart Disease and Atrial Fibrillation
